content:
In 2020, Lois and Dave Cho became the first Korean American winemakers in Oregon when they launched CHO Wines in the Willamette Valley. The fast-growing winery quickly amassed a following and received critical acclaim, but they kept fielding the same question: “What informs your palate for wine?”

The answer to that question grew to become so much more than they expected. The two kept thinking back to the Korean food they enjoyed as children, saying that they ultimately hoped for the bottles from CHO Wines to complement their heritage’s cuisine. But pondering their response revealed a more sobering reality: The Asian-American wine scene is far less appreciated than its culinary counterpart.

Considering their wine as something to be paired with Korean food sparked the idea of hosting a potluck for AAPI folks around the Willamette Valley. The brainstorming snowballed from there, and turned into a full-blown festival. In hopes of placing Asian American–made wine on the same level as food, the Chos officially launched AAPI Food & Wine in 2023.

“The first year, we hosted 12 Portland chefs and five Asian American Pacific Islander-owned wineries from the Willamette Valley,” Lois Cho says. “We had 1,000 people show up, and it was sold out.”

Though it came together in a matter of weeks, the inaugural event’s response was sentimental. “Multiple people came up to me with tears in their eyes,” Lois says. “I knew it was going to be a kick-ass party, but I didn’t realize that it was going to be so emotional.”

That emotional response was proof of concept. Since its debut, AAPI Food & Wine has held three annual walkaround festivals in Oregon, inviting participants to set up stalls with samples for attendees to learn and taste. Earlier this year, it inaugurated its expansion to the East Coast with a three-day-long celebration in New York City. Each of the events has been a near or total sell-out. Now, a group of board members handle the nonprofit’s operations, including secretary and volunteer director Sylvia Choi and vendor relations and events director Jane Barmore.

In the U.S., AAPI communities have been taught to assimilate to American culture and keep quiet to avoid scrutiny, Lois says. But after generations of repression, an outward embrace of Asian American food and wine was cause for celebration.

“A lot of our history has been about flying under the radar and not making a fuss,” she says. “This new generation is now really coming more into the spotlight and saying, ‘This is our heritage, and this is how it plays into food and wine.’”

The first Oregon festival featured beloved wineries like Hundred Suns Wine and Et Fille Wines, as well as Portland-based restaurants like Sun Rice and Matta. The nonprofit has since grown to amass a roster of other well-regarded chefs, winemakers, and collaborators, hosting events with industry pros like winemaker Sashi Moorman of Evening Land Vineyards and James Beard Award-winning bakers Jin Caldwell and Kyurim “Q” Lee of JinJu Patisserie. During its NYC residency this March, AAPI Food & Wine partnered with Atoboy, a Korean restaurant among the city’s culinary elite. With big-name affiliations and one expansion already under its belt, the nonprofit is ready for more growth.

“We’re already in chats about doing events in Los Angeles, Seattle, Chicago, D.C., and hopefully Austin at some point,” Lois says. “We keep getting the requests.”

Lois hopes to highlight chefs and winemakers outside of the Pacific Northwest and New York metropolitan areas with these expansions. After focusing on well-known chefs at previous festivals, she wants to include up-and-coming cooks who operate small brick-and-mortars or food carts.

And as the culinary scene increasingly celebrates AAPI cuisine, Lois sees that the wine industry is beginning to catch on. Some of the most celebrated sommeliers and beverage directors of today are AAPI-identifying, leading a pack of others to follow suit.

“There are a bunch of newcomers who are sharing their experiences getting into wine and pursuing their Master Sommelier certification,” she says.

Just as the first festival grew from a potluck, AAPI Food & Wine has expanded beyond anything Lois imagined. The community of participants, partners, and attendees the festival has corralled is the biggest driver in fueling its momentum, she says.

“Now, it’s like people don’t even know we’re involved in it,” she says. “They’re just like, ‘Oh my gosh, have you heard of AAPI Food & Wine? I’m like, ‘Yeah, my husband and I actually started it.’”

title: Next Wave Awards Industry Icon of the Year: Kimball House
summary:
Kimball House stands in a former train depot in the Atlanta suburb of Decatur, Ga. It gets its name from a historic Atlanta hotel. Its moniker was chosen to honor the long-gone hotel bars that drove the city’s cocktail culture at the turn of the 20th century. These elements help Kimball House share the history and traditions of a city which tend to gravitate toward contemporary design and aesthetic. Yet they’re not what make Kimball House such an enduring Atlanta institution.

content:
Kimball House stands in a former train depot in the Atlanta suburb of Decatur, Ga. It gets its name from a historic Atlanta hotel. Its moniker was chosen to honor the long-gone hotel bars that drove the city’s cocktail culture at the turn of the 20th century.

These elements help Kimball House share the history and traditions of a city which tend to gravitate toward contemporary design and aesthetic. Yet they’re not what make Kimball House such an enduring Atlanta institution. Rather, they are meant to be respectfully referential anecdotes for a space that began carving its own distinctive character from the moment it opened in 2013.

“When we opened, we wanted to make sure we were doing an homage without making it an amusement park,” explains Kimball House co-founder and beverage director Miles Macquarrie. “We also saw that so much of Atlanta had modern polish, and we knew we didn’t want that.”

The secret sauce allowing Kimball House to be a seamless portal linking past and present is its insistence to engage in honest hospitality. This is different from Southern hospitality, which can oftentimes be reduced to a cliched trope punctuated by y’alls and drawls. It’s a warm, familial form of service that’s meticulous in its execution but relaxed in its presentation, set in an environment that doesn’t take itself too seriously — it’s hard to be stuffy when there’s a taxidermied bobcat overlooking the space from a cozy nook. This formula shields their critically-acclaimed food menu from pretension, regardless of the dish’s ambitiousness.

While guests can feast on expected fare like sliced ribeye and oysters without feeling too fancy, they can also opt to dig into elevated dishes with distinctive regional elements to provide a touch of homespun flair, like trout with blue corn grits and okra or pork loin accompanied by green tomatoes and peaches. Kimball House’s must-have buttery Hawaiian rolls with peach preserves set a chic-yet-relaxed tone at the meal’s outset, regardless of the culinary direction the night takes.

Macquarrie’s bar program also provides a clean snapshot of this philosophy. The menu’s drinks draw equal inspiration from classic precision-driven techniques and modern technological innovation, underscored by a culinary approach accentuated by fresh ingredients grown in their on-site garden. This produces plenty of delicious, nerdy cocktails like a Fig & Honey Sour or a Cognac-based, force-carbonated take on the classic French 75.

“We use modern techniques, but we won’t mention them on the menu,” Macquarrie says. “To us, those techniques are just a component of a great drink.”

Kimball House’s glassware furthers such modesty. The venue presents drinks in a mismatched assortment of vintage vessels they’ve amassed through years of scouring Atlanta’s robust antique scene. The collection naturally plays into Kimball House’s easygoing homespun vibe, but it also allows the venue another avenue to connect with Atlanta’s past in a more intimate fashion.

“The glasses make you think of history. It may make you think what people were drinking in those glasses 30 or 40 years ago, or even longer,” Macquarrie says. “There’s a story in every glass, and using them shows that we care enough to share those stories.”

Such thoughtfulness is truly indicative of Kimball House’s devotion to honest hospitality, and this adherence fuels their iconic status. It also puts them in a position to help draw national attention to Atlanta and a cocktail scene that flies so under the radar, it’s practically subterranean. According to Macquarrie, any added attention is a bonus that supplements their main focus.

“Atlanta always takes a back seat to cities like New York and San Francisco,” he says. “I don’t know why, but that’s fine. After all these years, we still just want to run a good restaurant.”

title: Next Wave Awards Rising Drinks Brand of the Year: Still Austin Whiskey Co.

content:
In the whiskey world, if you’re doing everything yourself — if you’re not cutting any corners, if you’re trying to be a true original — it can take quite a while, perhaps even more than a full decade to become “up-and-coming.”

Such is the case with Still Austin Whiskey Co.

“It takes time. It does take time,” says Chris Seals, the CEO at Still Austin. “But it’s not just waiting around. Like, this is probably the most dynamic time in our lives, 15 years in.”

For Still Austin, it would take a retirement, state laws to be changed, a new sub-category to emerge, and we haven’t even got to all the toil of assembling a team, sourcing grains, fermenting, distilling, aging, bottling, and packaging.

It was back in 2012 when Cleveland Seals began looking for a retirement project and, hey, wouldn’t opening a whiskey distillery be fun? By that year, American whiskey was still in the early stages of explosive growth, going from 190 proof gallons produced in 2012 to well over 350 million by 2024 according to the TTB. Cleveland asked his son, Chris — who was working as an economist and risk manager at the time, perhaps aptly for this crazy endeavor — to join him. Chris thought success was unlikely and the time commitment would be immense, but at least the time would be spent with his dad, who he had struggled to forge a relationship with after coming out in his 20s.

Chris Seals wanted to live life as his true self and wanted to create a whiskey brand based on those values.

“You can’t be your true self when you fake it,” he says. “You have to let people see who you truly are and like that.”

That time with his father would initially start with research — traveling the country trying whiskeys. It was still quite difficult to start a distillery in Texas, until a 2013 law would allow for in-state distillers to sell their spirits directly to consumers as well as offer on-premise tastings.

By 2014, the Seals, along with their partners Andrew and Lisa Braunberg and Sal and Joanna Salinas, had broken ground on a facility in the St. Elmo neighborhood Austin. By 2017, head distiller John Schrepel, who had formerly run operations at New York’s Black Dirt Distillery, had distilled their first liquid using his own unique mashbills. Industry legend Nancy Fraley would advise on the maturation and blending using her signature élevage methods to help them in their grain-to-glass journey.

Yet even from the get-go, it was never solely about the liquid.

“There’s four things that we really want to give people,” says Seals. “We want them to feel deeply human. We want them to feel seen. We want them to feel free to express themselves. And we want them to feel the confidence to be distinct. If you can press those four, you are authentic.”

Still Austin would do this by focusing more on the people — their employees, their co-workers, their fellow artists, their customers — than on the liquid. The bottles have stunning, full-color labels painted by Texas artist Marc Burckhardt. Each label is meant to capture and honor the unique people that live among them in the so-called “Live Music Capital of the World,” whether artists, musicians, or naturalists. Seals has long aspired to use his burgeoning brand to create a new mythology for the creatives in the Austin community. He wanted to inspire these people whether they gave a damn about whiskey or not.

But that’s not to say that the whiskey isn’t stellar.

And this is pure Texas whiskey to be clear. It’s made from 100 percent Texas grains grown by Texas farmers and turned into Texas distillate aged in the unique climate of the hot and often erratic Texas Hill Country.

The Musician, Still Austin’s straight bourbon whiskey, uses the same chef-grade white corn that the area’s famous tortilla makers do. The result is a bourbon with a sort of a tropical piña colada note on the nose and palate of rich toffee and brown butter.

The Artist, their straight rye whiskey, employs a mashbill of 100 percent Brasetto rye, creating something wholly unique from the 95/5 rye you might be used to — theirs is like a chocolate-dipped cherry backed by nutmeg, clove, and a spicy cinnamon.

“There’s something special that goes on in our brains when we encounter something that astonishes us,” says Seals. “When the creativity is shocking, it releases a cocktail of hormones that induces wanting. One of the strongest triggers of that is individuality, novelty, and astonishment.” At Still Austin, they do that through flavor and with their one-of-a-kind painted label packaging. “And we do that with how we show up.”

Customers are showing up too. Last year saw some 100,000 visitors to the distillery. They come to hang with friends, to be a part of this unique community, to perhaps listen to live music on The Antone’s Stage at Still Austin. But the brand has also attracted fans from the connoisseurial community at large, who chase yearly one-offs like their Blue and Red Corn Bourbons and trade online for special single barrels, especially ones labeled “Nancy’s Pick.”

“That authenticity, it’s actually hard to do,” says Seals. “I think part of the reason that this award means so much to me right now is the things that we strive for now are much more human than they are simply a whiskey product.”

title: Next Wave Awards Brewery of the Year: Eckhart Beer Co.
summary:
Nicholas Meyer readily admits he’s stubborn. How else would one forge ahead opening a brewery amid today’s economic challenges and fickle, category-agnostic consumers? Or, to venture a step further, open that brewery centered entirely around traditional German and Czech lagers when American craft beer has for so long been fueled by a relentless cycle of novelty? content:
Nicholas Meyer readily admits he’s stubborn. How else would one forge ahead opening a brewery amid today’s economic challenges and fickle, category-agnostic consumers? Or, to venture a step further, open that brewery centered entirely around traditional German and Czech lagers when American craft beer has for so long been fueled by a relentless cycle of novelty? For Meyer, his staff, and the many customers who have found their new favorite gathering place at Eckhart Beer Co. in the Bushwick neighborhood of Brooklyn, that stubbornness has paid off.

“The hardest part of this process has been sticking to my guns,” Meyer says. “Now, anecdotally, we have people coming in all the time saying it’s so refreshing to see a brewery doing this.”

“This” is highlighting the Platonic ideal of lager from its homeland, and not chasing trends or ticking boxes with the hazy IPA, pastry stout, or fruited sour du jour.

“I’d thought about opening a brewery for a long time and felt like I didn’t have anything new to contribute [to those styles],” Meyer says. “It’s not that I wasn’t into them, but it just didn’t seem like the industry needed more of that.” When the lager-concentrated concept coalesced for Meyer, he thought, “I’d better do this now before anyone else does, and open it in New York.”

Meyer achieved that goal, and he probably doesn’t have to worry about too many other breweries being able to nail the balanced focus Eckhart embodies, between heightened hospitality and painstakingly executed lagers — all alongside other beverage options and a thoughtful food menu served in a well-appointed, welcoming space.

Much of what sets Eckhart apart thrives thanks to the all-star crew Meyer assembled. Operations manager Justin Sirois grew up in the hospitality industry, building a career in multimedia and starting a dedicated homebrewing habit before going pro in the brewing industry. Meeting Meyer seemed like a fated silver lining: recovering from an accident, he shared a hospital room with Meyer’s father. The more they talked, they talked beer; and the more they talked beer, they talked Meyer’s brewery vision.

“I shared that strongly,” Sirois says of Meyer’s passion for a lager focus. “I’d always been so excited by creative beers, but over time, I started wanting to simplify that and make the best versions possible.”

Eckhart’s brewer Adam Wolfe had been brewing in Sydney, Australia and Amsterdam for a decade — traveling Europe to study traditional styles and brewing methods — when he felt the pull back home to the East Coast. The post at Eckhart popped up and, again, had an air of kismet.

“You don’t see breweries just focusing on this style of beer very often, and it’s something I was really focusing on pretty heavily in Europe,” Wolfe says. “It seemed like a perfect opportunity.”

Meyer and Sirois began working together on the Eckhart concept in 2022. Construction on their facility in Bushwick began in April 2023, and their first beer was brewed in September 2024. The early stages of this process entailed fine-tuning what exactly the Eckhart beer program would be.

“There was no doubt in my mind about Helles Lager, any serious lager brewery has to brew a Helles,” Wolfe says. His personal favorite, the German Pilsner, was a lock. Then, he wanted to represent Czech styles; they landed on the “super flavorful, everyday workhorse beer” Czech Pale Lager, then rounded out the lineup with a Czech Dark Lager and Czech Amber Lager.

Eckhart’s core beers also include the Haus IPA, but it’s not this team’s style to brew anything just because they feel obliged. Theirs is a study in balance, flavor, and restraint just like the lagers it shares menu space with. Depending on what time of year you’re in the taproom, you’ll also find Festbier, Kölsch, Italian-style Red Lager, Gose, Grapefruit Radler, Baltic Porter, Czech-style Pils, West Coast Pils, and more.

The brand prioritizes hospitality right alongside brewing. Meyer’s background is in fine dining; he’s served as sous chef at Eleven Madison Park, Blue Hill, and Del Posto and instructed at The International Culinary Center. Any brewery he opened was going to go all-in on service.

Rachel Wood joined the Eckhart team as manager with 15 years of experience in hospitality, much of that being where she says her heart is, in breweries. She notes that Meyer’s vision of “narrow but deep” resonated with her: a dedicated focus, done with utmost intention.

Irene Hernandez joined Eckhart’s hospitality team as assistant taproom manager and lead bartender with her own appreciation for the streamlined beer concept along with some fresh perspective.

“Jared [Ferguson, Eckhart’s chef] and I are both Latinos, so we bring some Hispanic flair to the table,” she says. Hernandez’s main goal is to make sure everyone who walks through Eckhart’s doors feels welcome, beer connoisseur or not.

Wood shares that goal, helping introduce guests to the elevated service and beer traditions at Eckhart. The brewery uses Czech Lukr side-pull faucets to pour their beer. These taps enhance beer’s foam, creating a dense, velvety head jam-packed with aromas like a thick beer smoothie. They require training and technique to master, and manipulate into different pouring styles.

Wood and Hernandez bring Eckhart’s beer culture to life through events, too. On the second Saturday of each month, their all-day Kölsch Service transports patrons to Cologne or Dusseldorf beer halls. Kölsch service is hard enough to come by in the U.S.; Eckhart raises the bar by also offering the Dusseldorf-born Altbier style when in season.

Tying the beer and hospitality together is Eckhart’s noteworthy food program, which draws inspiration from drinking cultures across the globe. There’s crisp pork belly in aji verde sauce and a roasted beet salad with dried cherries, chili crisp, and lemon tahini alongside elevated German beer hall classics like a soft pretzel, bratwurst plate, brat dog — plus the vegetarian spin, a falafel dog, potato pancakes, Katsu-style chicken cutlet, and a decadent spaetzle gratin.

All it takes is a visit to Eckhart to sense that the magic comes as much from the team as it does from the satisfyingly bitter-leaning German Pilsner or refreshing yet malt-rich Czech Pale Lager.

“I didn’t know this was going to work when I started out, but the more we’ve added people to the team, it feels like if you just commit to something and you’re clear in communicating what you want to do, the right people who are also enthusiastic about that will find you.”

title: Next Wave Awards Brewer of the Year: Eamoni Collier
summary:
To Eamoni Collier, having a brewery isn’t just about beer. That might sound counterintuitive, but Collier’s bigger-picture vision of beer as a conduit to community-building and culture-celebrating is precisely what makes her stand out as the exceptional brewer she is. For Collier, the founder of Washington D.C.’s first Black woman-owned craft beer company Urban Garden Brewing, the epiphany came when she was honing her brewing chops at Right Proper Brewing Company.

content:
To Eamoni Collier, having a brewery isn’t just about beer. That might sound counterintuitive, but Collier’s bigger-picture vision of beer as a conduit to community-building and culture-celebrating is precisely what makes her stand out as the exceptional brewer she is.

For Collier, the founder of Washington D.C.’s first Black woman-owned craft beer company Urban Garden Brewing, the epiphany came when she was honing her brewing chops at Right Proper Brewing Company. Collier is also a musical artist, and to celebrate a song she was releasing, she collaborated with her teammates at Right Proper on a beer named for that single, “Strawberry High.” The brewery held an event for the debut of the strawberry milkshake IPA, brewed with hibiscus and rose petals.

“That’s when I realized it wasn’t just about the beer, it was about the experience of creating what’s behind the beer, and bringing people together when it’s done,” Collier recalls. “It clicked for me, ‘This isn’t just for bringing out beer lovers, but the whole community.” That was what Collier decided to build her own brand, Urban Garden, on. That, and exceptional beer.

A native Washingtonian, Collier started learning about the nuances of different beer styles before she could legally drink. She worked as a hostess at a distillery that also served beer in Savannah, Ga. while attending college there, and says the bartenders would have her smell beers to start learning their aromas without tasting them. After Collier moved back to D.C. and continued working in hospitality, she began making her own beer.

“I started homebrewing and hosting tastings in my uncle’s backyard,” she says. “Whenever we had cookouts or parties, people would ask, ‘Does Eamoni have her beer here?’”

As soon as she began brewing, Collier experimented with using botanicals. She’d pick them from her uncle’s garden and get them from local tea and herb shops.

“That was my cauldron,” she says of her brewing kettle. “I was making potions, there was a mystical vibe.” The botanicals — from chamomile to lavender — captured people’s attention, Collier adds. “They’d say, ‘Wow, this doesn’t even taste like beer.’” That got the wheels turning even before Collier landed her job at Right Proper and eventually brewed that Strawberry High IPA.

“You’d always see beer marketed toward men, but I was seeing women in my family say, ‘I don’t like beer, but I like this beer.’ I realized this was an untapped market.”

When the pandemic hit in 2020 and restaurants had to close down, Collier’s work in the hospitality industry temporarily came to a halt. She used the time to build a vision and business plan for her own brewing company. She wrote homebrew recipes and paid a production facility to scale, produce, and package them; then she’d self-distribute the beer.

The first beer Collier released in 2021 was Chamolite, essentially a blonde ale she dubbed a “Garden Ale” as it includes chamomile as well as honey. It sold so well from the jump that the business quickly blossomed into a full-blown contract brewing operation. She built her brand through regular events at spots throughout D.C., which not only introduced people to her beer but provided that outlet she valued for bringing people together. Before long, Collier realized she wanted her own permanent space. With help from family and investors, she opened Urban Garden on June 19, 2026.

Urban Garden’s location is serendipitous: It is the former address of Right Proper, where Collier’s brewing career took off. (Right Proper has moved to a different location.) It is also next door the Howard Theatre, where her grandfather Joe Tate would play saxophone with the house band. Collier has created the “Joe Tate Listening Lounge” in the taproom where she displays photos of her grandfather and other musicians as well as his sax. She also hosts GoGo brunches, GoGo being a D.C.-born funk subgenre Tate contributed to forming.

This homebase is an important one to have not just for the community she’s already begun building, but for the representation Urban Garden fosters as D.C.’s first Black woman-owned brewery.

“It’s bittersweet,” she notes. “It’s 2026, and we’re just now having a Black woman-owned brewery here.” For context, less than one percent of breweries are Black-owned across the United States. “The fact that it needs to be highlighted means we have so much work still to do, such a long way to go to get people the resources they need to do this,” Collier says. Having Urban Garden, she recognizes, can be motivational. To build on that, Collier enthusiastically welcomes brewers and would-be brewers to visit the taproom and ask questions.

Urban Garden is built around community; beer is what makes that mission possible and brings more people through the door every day. Collier’s beers straddle a balance between familiar and intriguing, approachable and exciting.

“I decided I’m just going to create my own styles,” she says. “Our IPA I call a ‘botanical IPA’ because the bitterness doesn’t come just from hops but from the lavender flower we use.” Urban Garden’s beer menu reveals Collier’s mastery of classic beer styles while also providing her with a canvas on which to paint fresh botanical flavors that interest beer geeks and engage new-to-beer guests. Roses Aren’t Dead Pale Ale is made with rose petals and rose hips; the Orange You Witty Witbier with sweet orange peel, ginger, and toasted coriander; and the Touch Grass! Pilsner with lemongrass.

D.C. has taken to Collier’s fragrant beers as well as Urban Garden’s positioning as a gathering place. It’s something the brewer and business owner only wants to keep expanding on, creating a hub for everyone from young adults to seniors, with good beer, good food, fun events, and even education and future mentorship programs.

“Community and culture have always been the driving vision,” Collier says. “I get teary-eyed thinking about it, but the perfect example was Juneteenth, our opening day. It was a perfect representation of D.C., an actual melting pot — men, women, and kids of all cultures.”

title: Next Wave Awards Retailer of the Year: Vesper Books and Wine
summary:

It’s a tough business to work in, as importers and distributors with highly allocated bottles can be selective in which markets they sell to. With Vesper Books and Wine, Symantha Duggan and Robert Wilson are part of a movement that’s bringing access to these wines to Detroit, a market that’s long gone overlooked.

content:
The world of natural wine boasts just a few hot spots around the United States: New York City, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Portland, Ore., Chicago, and Austin. It’s a tough business to work in, as importers and distributors with highly allocated bottles can be selective in which markets they sell to. With Vesper Books and Wine, Symantha Duggan and Robert Wilson are part of a movement that’s bringing access to these wines to Detroit, a market that’s long gone overlooked.

Vesper Books and Wine is part-wine bar, part-retail shop, and part-culinary bookstore, with the three separate areas of its space each blending seamlessly into one another.

Vesper began as Duggan’s dream of owning and operating a bookstore that she tinkered with for over a decade. She started her career in office roles across a few different industries — her interest in hospitality only came into the equation after she moved to Paris and fell in love with wine. When she moved back home to Detroit in 2019 and met Wilson, a pedigreed bartender who had helmed some of Detroit’s top cocktail bars, brainstorming for Vesper kicked into high gear.

Finding the location was a stroke of luck. The couple, both natives of the Detroit suburbs, were at a friend’s wedding when someone mentioned to Duggan that he owned a 19th-century building that once housed a Detroit Savings Bank. “It was a hyper-Detroit experience. Like, of course I would sit next to someone at a wedding that owns an old bank.”

The two spent the years leading up to Vesper’s opening in 2024 raising capital and renovating the space themselves with the help of some friends, artists, and an architect. Together, they built the retail store and bar on loans and grants. Elements of the former bank remain intact in the revamped space: Check-writing counters are now bar seats, and the old vault is now a private seating area.

From the start, Vesper aimed to bring something new to the city. Whether the by-the-glass list features a pour of Jean Foillard Beaujolais-Villages or a Marquette from Michigan, Wilson, who curates the shop’s wine selection, wants customers to learn something new each time they walk in.

“Michigan is a tough state to order in,” he says. “There are very few items available to us, so having an obscure bottle selection takes a lot of work. We want to introduce wines to people that they’re not normally going to see, like an Uruguayan orange.”

As much as the two want Vesper to bring new, unfamiliar wine and books to Detroit, Wilson and Duggan are also intentional about fitting into the store’s neighborhood. Detroit suffers from one of the highest poverty rates in the U.S., and the couple wants to be cognizant of serving the people in their community first and foremost.

Vesper Books and Wine is in Detroit’s Core City neighborhood, where the median household income is around $35,000, Duggan says. She and Wilson work tooth and nail to keep prices reasonable.

“We spend hours, hours, and hours each week, scouring through catalogs and magazines to make sure that what we have on our menu and on our shelves is of the highest quality, is accessible in language and in knowledge, and also meets the price point as much as we possibly can in today’s age,” she says.

Duggan, who spearheads the shop’s cookbook selection, also makes an effort to represent the many diasporas that make up Detroit’s ethnic fabric with what she stocks on the store’s shelves. Whereas the city is riddled with chain bookstores selling tens of thousands of titles, she wants Vesper’s point of view to be unabashedly Detroit.

The venue’s three prongs — wine bar, wine retail, and cookbook store — converge to become a “third space” for Detroiters. Vesper facilitates a Cookbook Club, which sends members individually selected recipe books and hosts potluck-style events where they can share featured dishes. Duggan and Wilson also put on book signings and pop-ups with high-profile food media personalities, such as Carla Lalli and Jon Kung, and small-production winemakers like Brent Mayeaux of Stagiaire Wine.

Though it’s just a year and a half old, Vesper has already amassed a wide audience of regulars, out-of-town visitors, wine-interested, and cookbook enthusiasts alike. While there’s still more ground to cover, Detroit’s once-disregarded wine presence is gaining steam: The city has seen the addition of acclaimed wine bars like Ladder 4 and Bar Chenin over the past several years, and it’s only poised to keep growing.

“We’re hitting a gateway right now where things are changing in the wine and books industry in Michigan,” Duggan says. “Wine is becoming more appreciated and available, and there are more niche books that are becoming available too. Now is the time.”

title: Next Wave Awards Sommelier of the Year: Matt Turner

The article Next Wave Awards Sommelier of the Year: Matt Turner appeared first on VinePair.
content:
When thinking of the qualities that make a “great” sommelier — meticulous knowledge of regions, grapes, soils; familiarity with the world’s top producers; and hospitable service — one attribute that often goes overlooked is curiosity. But flipping through the dense wine book at New York City’s Lei, bound in brown leather, embossed with lime-green text, and filled with eclectic bottles from across the globe, it’s clear that wine director Matt Turner is driven by curiosity above all else.

Turner’s eagerness to explore different topics didn’t necessarily start with wine. As a college student in Florida he dabbled in genetics, trumpet performance, and ancient Greek literature before selecting finance as his major. But when Turner was finally introduced to the world of wine in college, he was instantly hooked. For him, popular culture had always painted wine as a historic, artisanal product, but looking around on store shelves, all he would see was mass-produced, commercially scaled brands. This dichotomy spurred a quest to find the wines that spoke to the heart of the tradition, leading him to a friendly wine bar and shop near campus in Tampa.

“Whenever I had free time outside of school,” Turner recalls, “I would sit at the bar and get to know various people and talk to the staff.” These connections became Turner’s entryway into the industry, first with a gig in distribution and then picking up shifts at that same bar, where he eventually landed a full time job by the time he graduated college.

At work, every day was an opportunity to taste and learn. “The goal was to taste as much wine as possible,” Turner says. Riesling from the Rheinhessen, Northern Rhône Syrah, Willamette Valley Chardonnay, obscure skin-contact wines from the Czech Republic — he wanted to try it all. Though endless tasting might seem tiresome to most, Turner’s interest never waned, it only grew more intense. Looking to grow his career, the natural next step was moving to a bigger market — one like New York City.

Turner arrived in the Big Apple in mid-2020. Breaking into the wine scene during the pandemic was a little touch and go, until an enlightening dinner at the now-closed Niche Niche changed his course. The restaurant was known for hosting pop-ups featuring different wine personalities each night, with an ever-changing menu and accompanying wine pours. Amid lively discussions about the evening’s wines, Turner found himself chatting with Niche Niche owner Ariel Arce, an encounter that resulted in him joining the team at sister restaurant Air’s Champagne Parlor. Turner moved up through the ranks among the group, from trailing to somming at Air’s to taking on the head sommelier role at Niche Niche, and later opening Roscioli, Heroes, and Pearl Box, eventually becoming the beverage director for the latter.

Managing the beverage program and working with cocktails at Pearl Box, Turner felt an itch to get back to what he loved most about the industry — working hands-on to help customers explore the expansive world of wine. And what better setting could there be for interacting with guests than a small, 28-seat wine bar? With this goal, Turner joined owner Annie Shi and chef Patty Lee to open Lei, a wine bar and restaurant in Chinatown.

The team set out to create a space where diners feel welcome to drink what they want. “We thought, let’s make an interesting list that provides everything for everyone,” Turner says. “Affordable, accessible wines that are all quality at all price ranges.” This ethos was immediately evident when the warm, candlelit space started welcoming in customers in June 2025. Posts flooded in across social media platforms: collectors raving about Lei’s exceptional Burgundy and Champagne program; novices thrilled to find an approachable skin-contact by-the-glass pour from Greece; and fellow curious drinkers squealing with excitement to try bottles from China and Japan.

Though Turner acts as the wine director (which might be a hands-off role in most restaurants), Lei’s tight-knit structure allows each member of the team to be highly involved with guests. Sommeliers are servers, servers are sommeliers. Each person working the floor can tell you about the obscure Portuguese blend on the list, or walk you through six different cuvées from a top Burgundy producer. Because of this, the passion for wine reverberates through every corner of Lei.

For Shi, two of the central tenants for Lei’s wine program were to have a dynamic, broad-reaching list that provides access to all, and to feature wines that are always showing well at the table. To achieve this, Turner and the team are constantly tasting wine and discovering new gems to fill the list with. “The most important part is the enthusiasm of the people in the program to taste new wine,” he says.

Turner’s fervor for uncovering new, interesting producers and sharing them with the guests at Lei has also manifested as a series of pop-ups. Whether it be a by-the-glass takeover from Spain’s hot upstart winemaker Jorge Olivera or a meet and greet with wine pros spanning from smaller producers like Chile’s Roberto Henriquez to the export director for posh labels like Champagne Salon and Champagne Delamotte. He even recently organized a tasting exploring how wine evolves over time — pouring a Riesling from Kissinger-Bähr opened that day alongside the same bottle opened three, five, and seven days prior.

“I don’t always advertise these events a lot for a reason,” Turner admits. “Part of that is because I want people who are coming to Lei naturally to be confronted by a new, unexpected thing. To be encouraged to try something new, to meet a winemaker you might have never thought you would meet.”

In an industry that seems to funnel all interested drinkers to the same few regions and producers, Turner loves to push the guests at Lei to try more. But he emphasizes that the essential counterpart to curiosity is trust. The freedom to host these pop-ups comes from time establishing a relationship with the guests at Lei, building trust that the team will always be able to find the right wine for you.

title: Next Wave Awards Wine Professional of the Year: Matt Crafton
summary:
In 2003, Matt Crafton arrived at his first interview for a winery job in a full suit and tie. He’d just received an economics degree from the University of Virginia but yearned for a hands-on career with room for creativity. A total greenhorn in the wine industry, Crafton decided he’d cut his teeth as the cellar rat at any Virginia producer that he could convince to hire him.

The article Next Wave Awards Wine Professional of the Year: Matt Crafton appeared first on VinePair.
content:
In 2003, Matt Crafton arrived at his first interview for a winery job in a full suit and tie. He’d just received an economics degree from the University of Virginia but yearned for a hands-on career with room for creativity. A total greenhorn in the wine industry, Crafton decided he’d cut his teeth as the cellar rat at any Virginia producer that he could convince to hire him.

Now 23 years into the game, Crafton, president and winemaker at Chateau Montelena, proudly wears crew neck T-shirts and jeans to work — evidence of his personal and professional inclination for substance over style.

At the helm of such a historic estate, Crafton could easily rest on Chateau Montelena’s long-established laurels: The winery produced the Chardonnay that bested Burgundian competitors at the iconic 1976 Judgement of Paris and has since risen through the ranks as one of Napa’s foremost producers. Instead, he is nimble and ready to usher Chateau Montelena into the future, despite the headwinds that stand in the American wine industry’s way.

“The way we honor the past is not by dwelling on it,” he says. “We’d be doing a disservice to the people whose shoulders we stand on if we didn’t continue to innovate. They’d want us to get out in the world and bring our wine to new consumers.”

Crafton started his career at the bottom of the barrel at a winery in Williamsburg, Va., eventually becoming cellar master. After earning a second bachelor’s degree in viticulture and oenology at the University of California, Davis, Chateau Montelena’s CEO and owner Bo Barrett — son of Jim Barrett, who purchased the estate in 1972 — hired Crafton on a one-year contract to work in the lab in 2008. Crafton’s dedication helped him swiftly rise through the ranks. By 2010, he was promoted to overseeing all white wine production, then earned the position of head winemaker four years later. In January 2026, Barrett named Crafton president and winemaker.

With the wine industry facing a down market, Crafton thinks winemakers can either spend their time navel-gazing about the doom and gloom or reassess their strategy and reroute course. Crafton embraces the latter. To do so, he is ready to reject what the rest of the industry is doing — or, better yet, he’s unafraid to try something new.

Rather than leveraging the methods of the past, Crafton embraces innovative marketing tactics. He took some of Chateau Montelena’s club members on a trip to Iceland this year, and in the past, he traveled to Argentina, New Zealand, and elsewhere around the world with the winery’s patrons. The trips may not be on site in Napa Valley, he admits, but an affinity for Montelena’s wine is the common ground among the strangers, which affirms their relationship with the brand.

“You have to bring the story and bring the brand to your consumers,” he says. “When so many other wineries are pulling back on those initiatives and doing less market work, we’re doing more.”

He brings up the proverbial fork in the road: “When I see everyone stampeding in one direction,” he says, “I go in the other direction.” When rosé was all the rage in the 2010s, Crafton turned his shoulder to pink wine. And now, as a major portion of the industry leans into non-alcoholic wines, Crafton refuses to budge.

“We have to go guerrilla,” he says. “We’re not going to follow the established playbook. I don’t want to just play the game — I want to win the game.”

Following the uptick in sales in 2020 during the pandemic, Crafton says many of Chateau Montelena’s peers scaled up production — and, in turn, scaled down quality — a trend that he resisted. Chateau Montelena produces 40,000 cases a year, roughly identical to the estate’s volume in the 1980s.

While the rest of the industry channels all of their focus into regaining ground over the next few years, Crafton’s attention is on the long game. As many other wineries vie for shelf space at national chains to bolster sales, Crafton puts his efforts into small retailers because, as he puts it, “no one can sell small, independent brands like small, independent retailers.” He also rejects the current wave of discounting that’s swooping over the industry — a choice that may compromise the business’ short-term gains, but puts its brand value in a better position for years down the line.

“Slow, organic growth and wine quality are first and foremost,” he says. “That is how this brand will succeed. We’re not going to grow by making a frosé. I’ll leave that to somebody else.”

Crafton believes making and selling wine requires a robust combination of skills no single person can master, and the best way to get around that is to be OK with being uncomfortable. As he puts it: If a winemaker aims for comfort and safety, there’s a limit to their success.

“To me, average is failure,” he says. “Safety is not the goal. Success is the goal. I want this brand to be recognized not just as an incredible American wine story, but as the global brand. The only way we’ll accomplish that is by doing the hard things that other people won’t do.”

title: Next Wave Awards Winemaker of the Year: Alice Anderson
summary:
If you try to picture the romanticized image of winemaking in California, you might see rows of sun-drenched vineyards with ripe, juicy grapes hanging from each stem. The vines would be surrounded by a biodiverse environment of wildflowers and tall grass, with families of ducks and chickens bustling by as sheep graze their way down each alley. Though California’s intense sunshine fills the space with heat and light, swift, salty breezes serve as a reminder that the ocean is never too far away.

The article Next Wave Awards Winemaker of the Year: Alice Anderson appeared first on VinePair.
content:
If you try to picture the romanticized image of winemaking in California, you might see rows of sun-drenched vineyards with ripe, juicy grapes hanging from each stem. The vines would be surrounded by a biodiverse environment of wildflowers and tall grass, with families of ducks and chickens bustling by as sheep graze their way down each alley. Though California’s intense sunshine fills the space with heat and light, swift, salty breezes serve as a reminder that the ocean is never too far away.

For winemaker Alice Anderson, this is a snapshot of her daily life tending to Santa Barbara’s historic Ibarra-Young vineyard to make wine for her label, Âmevive. But in reality this picturesque ideal of winemaking is hardly easy to come by — it takes tremendous dedication and strenuous work. But with Anderson’s deep commitment to organic agriculture and sustainable practices, it’s the only way she’d have it.

Anderson’s winemaking career is rooted in her interest in farming. She attended Cal Poly for agriculture, but after her first class in dairy science didn’t speak to her, she wasn’t sure which direction she was interested in pursuing. It wasn’t until her mom, Eileen — who had long worked as a label designer for big wine brands like Gallo and Mondavi — suggested she look into the wine industry that she altered her course. “She set me up with a day of shadowing one of her clients,” Anderson says. “After experiencing the dynamic of working at a winery, I changed my major and never looked back.”

With a degree in viticulture and oenology, Anderson set off to New Zealand for an internship at Rippon, a biodynamic estate in Central Otago. “It was my first introduction to biodynamic farming and working with an estate model,” she says. “Working and being at a place where growing the grapes is so intertwined with the wine and talking about them as one entity, I fell in love with the whole process, with the energy of growing something.”

Anderson’s French roommate in New Zealand convinced her to move to France to dive further into wine culture, so she applied for an internship in the Rhône Valley with Famille Pierre Gaillard, where she later became the caviste. Eventually Anderson was pulled back to California and landed in Santa Barbara, working at Tyler Winery and other local projects.

The vision for Âmevive first came into view when Anderson saw a Facebook ad on a page for women winemakers. The post had an attached image of a Polaroid from the 1970s, depicting Charlotte Young riding her mule across her vineyard — one of the first vineyards planted in the Santa Ynez Valley — saying it was available for rent.

“I found Ibarra-Young in 2019 and everything really started there,” Anderson says. “It’s the soul of Âmevive.”

The vineyard was first established in 1971 with three acres of Syrah and Mourvèdre; Marsanne came into the fold in 1973, followed by Spanish varieties Tempranillo and Graciano in the ’90s. Each vine is own-rooted and the site has been farmed organically since 1993. The only stipulation listed when Anderson and her partner, Topher de Felice, agreed to lease the land was that they had to keep it organic. “I thought ‘OK easy,’” Anderson recalls, “that’s what we were excited about.”

Anderson immediately implemented her regenerative and biodynamic practices to the land, taking the vineyard to an entirely new level of sustainability. She wanted to reinvigorate the land’s soils and create the best possible environment for making wine. This meant giving space to other species beyond just grapes. She added pollinator rows and hedgerows and introduced sheep, ducklings, and chickens, working no-till and instead relying on the animals to graze the land. Anderson and de Felice run the 10 acre site on their own — they farm 20 acres total across the region — which Anderson admits is challenging work, but ultimately worth the effort.

“By putting in the extra work, not only does the land feel more energized, but because you are adding more life to a place, life starts to work with you — everything is in balance instead of fighting against you,” she says. “Farming is hard; you need a lot of grit. But if you lay the groundwork early, then there’s less insect and disease pressure and you don’t have to spray.”

When it comes to the winemaking itself, Anderson believes in letting the vineyard site express itself through the grapes, working with minimal intervention. “I worked in cellars with many reputable wineries for a long time, and now the winemaking is the easiest part for me,” she says. “We’ve done the hard work by growing the grapes. The goal for the wines is to not mess up the hard work that went into the vineyard.”

Anderson’s dedication to regenerative agriculture is apparent from the first sip — or even at first glance of the bottle, if you spend a moment to take in the beautiful watercolors (painted by her mother) that portray scenes from the vineyard, like hummingbirds, bees, wildflowers, and owls. The wines are vibrant, high-toned, and stunningly balanced. They land light on the palate, with bright acidity and lower ABVs than expected for something from the sunny Santa Ynez Valley, but still offer ample character, with fruit, savory notes, and texture all in harmony. Offerings range from a peppery, herbaceous Syrah to a vibrant, salty Albariño and a crowd-favorite blend of Roussanne, Marsanne, and Viognier, aptly named ‘Sundrop.’

Her passion for this approach to winemaking, one that prioritizes the health of the vineyards and soils, has inspired others across the industry. She speaks at events and conferences to share advice on organic agriculture and frequently shares her farming adventures on Instagram, with videos of her weeding rows or tending to her sheep, to give access to consumers on what goes into making her joyful, lively wines.

title: Next Wave Awards Winery of the Year: 00 Wines
summary:
In an industry with as much history and tradition as wine, producers are often eager to share how many generations their family has been in the business, how old and storied their estate is, or their impressive resume of winemaking education and experience working harvests across the globe. But the way Chris and Kathryn Hermann, the couple behind Oregon’s 00 Wines, see it, entering the industry as newcomers was one of their greatest advantages.

The article Next Wave Awards Winery of the Year: 00 Wines appeared first on VinePair.
content:
In an industry with as much history and tradition as wine, producers are often eager to share how many generations their family has been in the business, how old and storied their estate is, or their impressive resume of winemaking education and experience working harvests across the globe. But the way Chris and Kathryn Hermann, the couple behind Oregon’s 00 Wines, see it, entering the industry as newcomers was one of their greatest advantages.

Before starting 00 Wines in 2015, Kathryn was entrenched in the world of tech startups and Chris was a lawyer in the Willamette Valley, working with both local and international wineries. Though tangentially absorbing information about vineyard sites through client deals, the two had no experience making wine, just a mutual love for enjoying a great bottle of Chardonnay. Spending many evenings savoring an unctuous Burgundy or exploring producers from the U.S., it was clear Chris and Kathryn felt so much passion for the grape variety, the only thing left to do was try to make it themselves.

“The core of 00 Wines starts with us coming to this with a beginner’s mind,” Chris says. “We didn’t go to wine school, our family didn’t own a vineyard for 200 years. People often come to this industry with a context, a fixed architecture. We had to create our own.”

What the pair did have, though, was a clear goal in mind. “I had a vision of what I wanted the wine — particularly the Chardonnay — to look like, taste like, and feel like,” says Chris. “So from there, it’s figuring out what the pieces are to start to assemble the product that has all of these aspects. It’s about deconstructing the 150 steps from the vineyard to the bottle.”

Chris’ father was an esteemed plant geneticist at Oregon State, which imbued Chris with a lot of state pride, but also drew his interest to the scientific method. Chris applied this systematic approach to making wine, testing as many variables as possible to see what could get the wine closest to their vision. “That’s why we didn’t buy a vineyard,” he says. “We don’t know if that works best with high elevation, low elevation, east facing, west facing, sedimentary soil, volcanic soil, certain clones, grafted, ungrafted. So I assembled a giant matrix of all of these factors and just started testing them.” The duo painstakingly assembled trials to assess each factor, from vineyard site to barrel selection, determined to bring their dream Chardonnay to life.

While Chris and Kathryn wholly embraced their building-it-from-the-ground-up philosophy, that doesn’t mean they don’t value expertise. They also tapped famed consulting winemaker Pierre Millemann and hired Léa Lafon, who has deep family history in Burgundy’s Meursault region, to provide guidance.

In studying their favorite bottles of Chardonnay, one theme that clearly stood out was the use of the unconventional “black Chardonnay” method. The technique maximizes exposure to oxygen early in the process, turning the pressed grape juice into a murky, dark brown. It’s shocking at first, but over the next few months, the wine returns to a golden color, and is left with a remarkable complexity. Many winemakers would consider this approach risky — but the Hermanns were tenacious in their pursuit of excellent Chardonnay, willing to experiment and try anything to reach that perfect texture and energy.

“Much of what we do is not typical and sort of idiosyncratic,” Chris says. “That’s what causes us to be a unicorn. No one else is doing what we’re doing because they didn’t go through our process. And that’s why our wines have a distinctive signature.”

Though the industry was reluctant to embrace the newcomers at first, the wine’s unique style made it quickly stand out among the world’s top collectors. “People weren’t even willing to taste the wine at the beginning because we weren’t in the industry,” Chris says. “But we were incredibly persistent. What we began doing in the beginning was blind tastings with somms of our Chardonnay against bottles from Burgundy’s Coche-Dury. They would taste and you would see this look come over their face. Sometimes they would get it right, sometimes they wouldn’t.”

The wine first found its most dedicated audience through some high end Burgundy collectors, known for seeking out distinctive Chardonnays from small producers across the globe. In 2020, they recall getting a call from the head sommelier of the French Laundry who had tried the bottles that guests brought in as corkage and wanted to buy a case of every SKU. At that point, word was spreading about their wines.

What’s remained consistent through 00’s journey is its undying commitment to Chardonnay — though it also produces focused expressions of Pinot Noir. Chris and Kathryn have expanded the operation to Burgundy and Champagne, eager to have a foothold in each of the world’s premier terroirs for the white grape variety.

Though the production has scaled up from the winery’s first vintage of 250 cases with spray-painted labels — 00 now makes about 5,000 cases in Oregon — it remains a boutique operation, with Chris and Kathryn laser-focused on each aspect, from production to sales. As the wines have received more accolades and allocations have become more difficult for buyers to come by, the Hermanns have never rested on their laurels. Instead, they use their newfound platform to bring attention to the potential for great Chardonnay in the Willamette Valley, hosting wine dinners and tastings around the world, from Charleston, S.C. to Singapore, to showcase the incredible single-vineyard expressions coming from the humble Oregon region.

“That’s why we’re so specifically passionate about the Willamette,” Kathryn says. “The monks found out the great terroirs of Burgundy, but the greatest vineyards of the Willamette Valley haven’t been written in stone yet. It’s an exciting time to be on the cutting edge with other people in the region.”
